To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the expected relative risk of disease in a relative of a proband is a function of the population incidence of disease, the sex ratio, the liability correlation (r) between relatives, the sex of the proband, and the threshold for disease in the population.
a higher incidence in females than in males is not consistent with a multifactorial model, unless it is accompanied by a higher incidence in female relatives than in male relatives.
the expected RR is higher in relatives of the low risk vs the high risk proband sex, and the RR is a function of the sex ratio and r.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new approach to the study of the genetic etiology of disease, based on the use of the Multifactorsial-Polygenic model, which is applicable to diseases with a complex etiology, such as diabetes, schizophrenia, and hypertension.
the development of a new method of analysis that will be useful in testing hypotheses regarding the etiology of disease.
the development of a simple test of this model when two different thresholds can be identified.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Multifactorical-Polygenic Model is not consistent with the observed sex ratios for the majority of the psychiatric disorders studied to date.

the Multifactorical-Polygenic Model provides a reasonable explanation for a wide range of sex ratios in population incidence and the corresponding expected RRs to relatives of low risk and high risk sex proband.
a sex difference in the population incidence of a disorder does not support or refute a multifactorial-polygenic model for its etiology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a simple test of a Multifactorial Model can be made by examining the sex ratio of population incidence and comparing it to the RR of relatives of probands in the high risk sex vs relatives of probands with the low risk sex.
a simple test of sex differences in incidence can be used to test the Multifactoric-Polygenic Model.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Multifactoral-Polygenic Model is consistent with the observed sex differences in incidence for many disorders.
the Multifactoral-Polygenic Model is not a viable explanation for the sex differences in incidence and risk to relatives of probands observed in most complex disorders.

the Multifactoral-Polygenic Model provides a useful framework for understanding the relationship between population incidence, sex differences in population incidence, and the risk of relatives of affected probands.
